--- title: "Methods, in plain language" --- This page explains the four main methods behind the maps on this site, for a reader who is not a spatial analyst. Each one gets a plain definition, a worked example, and a note on what it can and cannot tell you. The full processing log, every parameter value, and the numbered decisions live in [`docs/methodology.md`](https://github.com/K-bsub/bay-area-wildcats/blob/main/docs/methodology.md). One idea runs through all four, and it is worth stating once at the top: **a record is not the animal.** Every method here starts from points that people reported — where a puma or a bobcat was seen or photographed. People do not look everywhere equally. So each method is, in part, a way to deal with that unevenness. Two of the methods below describe the records; one tries to remove the effort from them; one does not use the records at all. Keeping track of which is which is the whole point of the Effort page. --- ## Kernel density (KDE) **What it is.** Kernel density turns a scatter of points into a smooth surface. At every place on the map it asks: how many records are near here, and how near? Close records count for more than far ones. The result is a heat surface — warm where records cluster, cool where they are sparse. ![A worked kernel-density surface. The green circles are the raw point records. The grey bands are the density surface built from them — darker where points are dense, fading outward. Two dense cores are joined by a lower-density bridge, with a small outlying blob below. The bandwidth sets how far each point's influence spreads, and so how much the cores merge or stay separate.](media/images/kde_method.png){#fig-kde-method fig-alt="Green point records over grey nested density contours, two dense cores linked by a lighter bridge" width="70%"} *Illustration from [Spatial Analysis Online](https://www.spatialanalysisonline.com/HTML/density__kernels_and_occupancy.htm) (de Smith, Goodchild & Longley), used to show the method. It is not Bay Area cat data.* **The one setting that matters: bandwidth.** Bandwidth is the width of the smoothing. A narrow bandwidth hugs each point tightly and gives a spiky surface; a wide bandwidth blurs the points together into broad zones. The choice changes the map, so it must be made on a rule, not by eye. ::: {.callout-tip title="Worked example — the two cats used different bandwidths, on purpose"} For **bobcat**, an automatic selector (`bw.ppl`) passed the pre-set rule and chose a bandwidth of about **1,110 m**. Bobcat records are dense, so a tight smoothing still gives a stable surface. For **puma**, the same automatic selectors failed the rule — they returned values so small (as low as 49 m) that the surface would have been a scatter of pinpricks, not a density. So the bandwidth was set from biology instead: about **5,000 m**, roughly a puma home-range scale. This is why the puma density map shows broad warm regions, not sharp spots. ::: **What it can and cannot tell you.** KDE shows where records concentrate. It does **not** show where animals are, because the records are effort-shaped — warm can mean "many pumas" or "many observers." On this site the KDE surfaces are always read with that caveat, and the puma KDE is used only as a cross-check, never as a distribution result. --- ## Hot spots (Getis-Ord Gi\*) **What it is.** A hot-spot statistic asks a sharper question than KDE: is the clustering here **more than you would expect by chance?** For each open-space unit, Gi\* compares that unit **and its neighbours** against the whole study area. A unit with a high count, surrounded by other high-count units, becomes a statistically significant **hot spot**. The reverse — low counts among low counts — is a **cold spot**. **"Neighbours" has to be defined.** A unit's Gi\* score depends on which units count as its neighbours. Here, neighbours are units within a set distance (about **6,342 m**), with a floor so that even a remote unit still has some neighbours to compare against. **Why the correction matters.** Testing over a thousand units at once means some will look "significant" by pure luck. A false-discovery-rate correction (Benjamini-Hochberg) tightens the bar so the surviving hot spots are ones you can trust are real clustering, not chance. ![The Getis-Ord Gi\* flow, panel by panel. **Input data** — a value per unit (here median income, a generic example). **Z-scores** — each unit scored on how far its neighbourhood sum sits from the study-area average; strong positive (brown) and strong negative (purple) stand out. **P-values** — how likely each score is by chance. **Hot spots** — the final map, keeping only units that pass the significance bar: red are hot (high-value clusters), blue are cold (low-value clusters), pale is not significant.](media/images/hotspot_method.png){#fig-gistar-method fig-alt="Four-panel Getis-Ord Gi* workflow: input data, Z-scores, P-values, and final hot-spot map" width="85%"} *Illustration from the [UCGIS GIS&T Body of Knowledge](https://gistbok-ltb.ucgis.org/current/concept/AM-03-058) (Hot Spots and Getis-Ord Gi\* Analysis). The example maps income, not wildlife — the method is the same; on this site the value is the puma or bobcat record count.* ::: {.callout-tip title="Worked example — the effort check on top"} A record hot spot has two possible causes: real animals, or hard surveying. So each hot spot is cross-read against a **map of survey effort**. If a unit is a record hot spot **and** an effort hot spot, it is flagged **suspect** — it may just be where people looked. If it is a record hot spot but **not** an effort hot spot, it is **trusted**. On the Effort page you can see this split drawn directly: solid units are trusted, dashed units are suspect. ::: **What it can and cannot tell you.** Gi\* tells you where clustering is stronger than chance, and — with the effort check — how much of that is likely real. It still rests on the same effort-shaped records, so the effort flag is part of the result, not a footnote. --- ## Occupancy modelling **What it is.** Occupancy modelling is the one method here that tries to **remove** the effort problem instead of just flagging it. It splits the question into two parts and fits them in order: 1. **Detection.** Given that a bobcat is present in a unit, how likely was it to be *recorded*, given how much people surveyed there? This is fitted first, with presence held constant, so the model learns the shape of the effort signal. 2. **Occupancy.** With the detection part fixed, the model then estimates the probability the animal is actually **present**, corrected for that effort. The output is a presence surface that has the survey effort taken out — which is why it can, and does, disagree with the raw record density. The two parts are two linked equations. For a unit $i$ and a visit $j$: $$ \underbrace{z_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\psi_i)}_{\text{occupancy: is the unit occupied?}} \qquad \underbrace{y_{ij} \mid z_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(z_i \, p_{ij})}_{\text{detection: was the animal recorded, if present?}} $$ - $\psi_i$ is the probability the unit is **occupied** — what we want. - $p_{ij}$ is the probability of **recording** the animal on a visit, *given* it is present. This is where survey effort enters. - $z_i$ is the true (hidden) presence, 0 or 1. The term $z_i\,p_{ij}$ encodes the key rule: **you can only detect what is there** — if $z_i = 0$, no record is possible, and a non-record where $z_i = 1$ is a *missed* detection, not an absence. Each side is modelled on covariates through a logit link — occupancy on habitat ($\text{logit}(\psi_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i}$) and detection on effort ($\text{logit}(p_{ij}) = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \, \text{effort}_{ij}$). Fitting the detection side first is what lets the model tell "the animal was absent" apart from "nobody looked." ::: {.callout-tip title="Worked example — bobcat"} The bobcat detection part was fitted first. A term for recording effort (the number of prior records in a unit) beat a no-effort model by a wide margin (about 408 AICc units — a very strong preference), confirming effort really does shape the raw records. With that fixed, the presence model was fitted over **845** open-space units. The result is the ψ (psi) surface on the Bobcat page — and it barely correlates with the raw density map (r = 0.075), because the model pulled the effort signal out. That disagreement is the method working, not failing. ::: **Why puma does not get this.** Occupancy modelling needs enough repeat records per unit to separate detection from presence. Puma records are too few and too obscured for a defensible fit, so the puma track uses connectivity (below) instead. This was a planned fork, not a shortfall. **What it can and cannot tell you.** Occupancy gives the cleanest presence estimate on the site, but only for bobcat, and only where enough units had repeat surveys — 284 units could not be modelled and are drawn as a distinct grey, never as "low occupancy." --- ## Cost-corridor (puma connectivity) **What it is.** The puma corridor is built from the **landscape**, not from records. It answers a movement question: if a puma travels between two large habitat cores, which route costs it the least? "Cost" here means difficulty of movement — open built-up land and busy roads are expensive to cross; forest and shrub are cheap. It is a three-step chain, and the map below shows all three. 1. **Resistance surface (the input).** Every 1 km cell is scored 1–100 for how hard it is to move through. The score is a weighted blend: **45% human modification, 40% land cover, 15% slope**, with busy roads overriding the blend where they cross. 1 is freely permeable (good forest); 100 is a wall (dense city, a major freeway). 2. **Cost-corridor surface (the output).** From the resistance surface, the model accumulates the total cost of routing between the two cores, in both directions. Low values trace the preferential route; high values are off-route. ::: {.callout-note title="What 'least-cost' actually means"} Think of the resistance surface as terrain where every 1 km step has a price — cheap through forest, dear across a freeway. The **least-cost path** is the route between the two cores whose **total price is lowest**, the same idea as a sat-nav finding the shortest drive, except the "distance" is movement difficulty, not kilometres. The algorithm works outward from a core, giving every cell its *cumulative* cost — the cheapest running total to reach it from the core. Do this from **both** cores and add the two surfaces, and each cell then holds the cost of the best route *through* it from core to core. That summed surface is the cost-corridor. The single cheapest line through it is the least-cost path; the low-cost **slice** around that line is the swath. A swath is used, not the bare line, because the exact line is a fragile artifact — shift one weight slightly and it hops a cell — while the slice is stable and honest about that uncertainty. ::: 3. **The swath (the published product).** The swath is simply the **lowest-cost slice** of the cost-corridor surface — the cheapest ~5% of cells to move through (a narrower core ~2% inside it). That slice, drawn as a band, is the corridor you see on the Puma page. ::: {.callout-note title="Why the corridor uses no records"} Because resistance is built only from land cover, human modification, slope, and traffic, the corridor never "sees" where pumas were reported. That is deliberate: it means when the corridor lands on the observed record density (the Effort page convergence finding), the agreement was not built in — it is evidence the pattern is real, not an effort shadow. ::: The map below shows the chain. The resistance surface (the input) underneath, the cheapest-route cost-corridor over it, and the two-tier swath outline on top — so you can read "the swath is the lowest-cost slice of this surface" directly. ::: {.cell} ::: {#fig-cost-corridor .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` The puma connectivity method, in three layers. Base: the movement-resistance surface (1 = freely permeable, 100 = near-impassable), built from human modification, land cover, slope, and major roads — no records used. Middle: the cost-corridor surface, the accumulated least-cost of routing between the two habitat cores. Top: the two-tier swath outline — the lowest-cost slice of that surface (core ≤ q2%, context ≤ q5%), which is the corridor published on the Puma page. Both rasters are published at the 1 km grain the sensitive-data policy requires. This is a method illustration, not a result. ::: ::: You can toggle the three layers with the control at top-right — turn the resistance base off to see the cheapest-route cost-corridor alone, or turn everything off but the swath to see the published corridor. The point of stacking them is to make the chain legible: the corridor is not drawn by hand, and it is not drawn from sightings; it falls out of the landscape, one step at a time. ::: {.callout-important title="A method illustration, not a result"} This map is here to explain how the corridor is built. The corridor **result** — where it runs, where it crosses roads, and how it reads against the record density — is on the Puma and Effort pages. The exact route has some play in it (about 1.5 km, tied to the human-modification weight); the two-tier swath, not the centre-line, is the honest product. ::: --- ## Where the detail lives Every choice on this page — the bandwidth rule, the neighbour distance, the model sets, the resistance weights and their sources, and the sensitivity checks that tested them — is recorded as a numbered decision in [`docs/methodology.md`](https://github.com/K-bsub/bay-area-wildcats/blob/main/docs/methodology.md), with the data sources in [`docs/data-sources.md`](https://github.com/K-bsub/bay-area-wildcats/blob/main/docs/data-sources.md) and the layer schemas in [`docs/data-dictionary.md`](https://github.com/K-bsub/bay-area-wildcats/blob/main/docs/data-dictionary.md).
